name: 天ぷら新宿つな八 大丸東京店
address_ja: 〒100-6701 東京都千代田区丸の内1-9-1 大丸東京店12F
cuisine: Edomae tempura on the 12th floor of the Daimaru department store above Tokyo Station's Yaesu north exit — sets of prawn, squid, conger, shellfish and vegetables fried to order in sesame oil, closing with kakiage and a choice of ten-chazuke or a small tendon; roughly ¥3,000 at lunch, ¥5,000 at night
neighborhood: Marunouchi 1-9-1, 12F of Daimaru Tokyo (GranTokyo North Tower) — 3 min on foot from the JR Tokyo Station Yaesu north exit and 3 min from Tokyo Station on the Tokyo Metro Marunouchi line
hours_raw: 11:00～22:00（L.O.21:00）　※ランチメニューは14:00（L.O.14:00）まで、食材の入荷状況により終了が早まる場合あり　定休日：不定休（大丸東京店に準ずる）
gf_detail: A tempura specialist: every course is wheat batter, and the kakiage that closes each set is batter-bound. The tentsuyu, the ten-chazuke and the small tendon are all built on ordinary wheat soy sauce, and one fryer serves the whole counter. The house's only oil claim is that it has fried in sesame oil since it opened — a flavour choice, not an allergen one. No gluten-free item, no wheat-free line, nothing published about wheat handling.
vegan_detail: The sets are built around prawns, squid, conger and shellfish, several open with sashimi, and the tentsuyu is a bonito dashi. Vegetable pieces exist inside the sets but there is no vegetable-only course, no plant-based dipping sauce, and the fryer is shared with fish.

roles: 三代目 代表取締役 — third-generation president, 株式会社綱八
chef_bio.origin: Tokyo; the family's original shop is the Shinjuku Sōhonten, still trading
chef_bio.background: This counter is a branch, but of an unusually old family firm. The company's own chronology dates the beginning to 1922, when the founder Kyūzō opened a tempura shop called 網八 (amihachi, 'net eight'); enough customers misread 網 as 綱 that the name つな八 stuck and the shop adopted it. A stand-and-eat tempura counter, 立食 天麩羅 綱八, followed in 1924; the building was pulled down in 1944 under wartime forced evacuation; the family kept itself going in 1945 selling manjū and shaved ice, and rebuilt the tempura shop on its present Shinjuku site in 1948. The first branch opened in the Shinjuku station building in 1964, the firm incorporated in 1981, and it marked its centenary in 2024 with 33 shops nationwide as of 2020. Hisaya Shimura is the third generation: born 1960, a Keio commerce graduate, he joined in 1983 and was given a small branch in Tsuchiura, Ibaraki, then found himself effectively running the company six months later when his father — the second-generation Keisuke Shimura — had a stroke. He formally became president in 1999 at 39. He describes his father as a charismatic one-man operator and says he wrote the company credo around 2000 precisely to move the firm off that dependence. He is also candid about what Tsunahachi is for: most of the roughly forty member shops of the Tokyo tempura association Tōtenkai are owner-run rooms charging ¥10,000–20,000 a head at night, and he deliberately sets Tsunahachi at ¥3,000–6,000 so that tempura reads as an everyday meal. The kitchen's signature oddities — deep-fried ice cream, whole clams fried in the shell (蛤の姿揚げ), oyster with green pepper — were his father's inventions and are still on the boards.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「おいしさに真心をそえて」 — flavour with sincerity attached. The company deliberately keeps no service manual, on the grounds that what satisfies each guest differs.
chef_bio.specialty: Sesame-oil Edo-style tempura at accessible prices, plus the house's own inventions: deep-fried ice cream, whole clam, oyster with green pepper.

anecdotes.text: The name is a misreading the shop decided to keep. The founder's 1922 shop was 網八 (amihachi); customers read the character as 綱 (tsuna), and it became つな八.
Deep-fried ice cream — now a standard tempura dessert across Japan — was invented by this company's second-generation president.
Shimura had a bank job lined up until his father asked whether he intended to become its chairman; they argued, and he joined the family firm instead.

name: eric'S by Eric Trochon
address_ja: 〒100-6505 東京都千代田区丸の内1-5-1 新丸の内ビルディング5階
cuisine: A wine bistro on the 5th floor of the Shin-Marunouchi Building, menu designed by M.O.F. chef Éric Trochon — pâté de campagne, sea-bream carpaccio, moules marinière, bavette steak and a daily fish or meat plate, with about ten French wines by the glass; weekday set lunches ¥1,700–¥2,500, lunch courses ¥3,800–¥6,200, dinner courses ¥9,300–¥14,900, à la carte mains ¥3,200–¥3,400
neighborhood: Marunouchi 1-5-1, 5F of the Shin-Marunouchi Building — 1 min from Tokyo Station, directly connected underground; nearest subway is Tokyo Station on the Tokyo Metro Marunouchi line
gf_detail: No gluten-free claim of any kind on the restaurant's own site. Wheat is all over the published menu — baguette comes with the set lunches, there is a spaghetti and a paella section, fish and chips, panisse aside, and desserts include a Mont Blanc and a gavotte-based chocolate. Nothing indicates a separate fryer or separate pasta water. There are genuinely gluten-free-shaped dishes on paper (carpaccio of the day's fish, moules marinière, the bavette steak, cheese and charcuterie plates, contract-farm pickles), so a diner who can eat in a shared kitchen has real choices — but the sauces are unpublished, this is a French kitchen where flour-thickened sauces are routine, and nobody has documented how they handle wheat. Treat as ask, and ask in advance.
vegan_detail: A French bistro whose menu is charcuterie, cheese, fish and meat. The plant-based items that exist are incidental — 契約農家の野菜のピクルス (contract-farm vegetable pickles ¥700), ひよこ豆のパニス (chickpea panisse ¥800), mixed olives, paprika cashews, dried fruit — and the panisse is fried in a shared fryer. There is no vegan course, no published vegan set, and the salad is 'chef's choice'. Enough to drink wine over, not enough for a meal.

chef_bio.chef_name: Éric Trochon (エリック・トロション)
roles: supervising chef / menu designer for eric'S by Eric Trochon
chef_bio.background: Trochon is the name on the door, not the man at the stove in Marunouchi: Japanese listings for the restaurant describe it as 監修 — supervised by, or designed by, him — and the Japanese trade press consistently frames it that way. He is worth the record anyway. Born in Paris in 1964, he took the Meilleur Ouvrier de France in 2011, the award Japanese writers translate as 'France's living national treasure', and he runs his own Paris restaurants: Semilla in Saint-Germain, later Solstice, which holds a Michelin star. His connection to Japan predates this room — from 2014 he was advisory chef to the French restaurant Pirouette at Toranomon Hills, and Tabelog reviewers describe him as a 親日家, a confirmed Japanophile. The French Cuisine Culture Centre's profile of him is unusual in that it barely leads with cooking: it describes a man who treats creativity as a life philosophy and works as a consultant across food generally, as a professor at his own alma mater FERRANDI (the culinary school attached to the Paris chamber of commerce), and as a practitioner of 'design culinaire' — an approach to food as design that he has taught in a FERRANDI MOOC with the food designer Marc Bretillot that drew over 4,000 students. He has collaborated with Paul Bocuse, Joël Robuchon, Pierre Gagnaire and Alain Senderens, and produces events for luxury brands. The Marunouchi brief he set is narrower and honest about itself: 「今のパリを切り取った日本のビストロ」 — a Japanese bistro that cuts out a slice of present-day Paris, standard bistro dishes plus whatever Paris is currently eating, arranged 'Éric-style'. The room is operated by the Marugo Group (株式会社ワルツ), a roughly 25-shop Tokyo wine-bistro group centred on Shinjuku 3-chōme, which opened two restaurants in the Shin-Marunouchi Building in 2017.
chef_bio.philosophy: Creativity expressed in every available form — cooking, teaching, consulting, 'design culinaire' — rather than confined to a single restaurant.
chef_bio.specialty: Present-day Paris bistro cooking with about ten French wines always open by the glass; the ¥9,300 eric'S dinner course is the house statement.

anecdotes.text: The FFCC profile notes he taught a FERRANDI online course in 'design culinaire' with food designer Marc Bretillot that attracted more than 4,000 students.
Before Marunouchi he was advisory chef to Pirouette at Toranomon Hills from 2014 — the Tokyo connection is a decade old.
The dining room faces Tokyo Station through a wall of windows; the operator's listing sells the view of the Marunouchi skyline as much as the food.

Ikyu and gnavi both describe the Marunouchi restaurant as 監修 (supervised) by him. Marunouchi.com lists it as a tenant at 丸の内1-5-1 新丸ビル.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Shared kitchen with a pasta and paella section, a fish-and-chips plate and a fried chickpea panisse. No dedicated fryer or separate pasta water is claimed.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Charcuterie and cheese dominate the small-plate menu; the few plant dishes come out of the same kitchen and fryer as the meat.

positives.text: The full menu with prices is published, so a diner can plan before arriving rather than negotiating at the table.
Courses are pre-booked (the eric'S and Luxe lunch courses are 要予約), which gives the kitchen notice for a dietary request.

cultural_comfort.note: Directly connected to Tokyo Station, open continuously from 11:00 to late, with a café slot in the afternoon and no dress code published — an unusually low-friction French room for the district. Reservations run through Ikyu, Tabelog and gnavi, all of which have English paths; walk-in for the weekday set lunch, which is explicitly not reservable. Prices are transparent: ¥1,700 for a bavette lunch, ¥9,300 for the dinner course. The site is Japanese-only, but the operator is a large Tokyo group used to visitors.

GF raised nowhere by the shop and left at 'ask'; vegan left at 'limited' with the specific dishes named.

name: 恵比寿 土鍋炊ごはん なかよし 丸の内iiyo!!店
address_ja: 〒100-0005 東京都千代田区丸の内1-4-1 丸の内永楽ビルディング B1F
cuisine: A teishoku diner-cum-izakaya in the iiyo!! basement floor of the Marunouchi Eiraku Building: rice cooked to order in a donabe clay pot with free refills, a monthly-changing set menu of grilled mackerel, nikujaga, karaage and chicken nanban with miso soup and small dishes, and no chemical seasonings; lunch sets around ¥1,000–¥1,500, a 1.5-gō clay pot of seasonal rice ¥1,800 at night
neighborhood: Marunouchi 1-4-1, B1F of the Marunouchi Eiraku Building (the iiyo!! dining floor) — 5 min from Ōtemachi station (85 m from the Ōtemachi exit), 10 min from Tokyo Station
gf_detail: Unusually for a teishoku chain, the operator publishes a downloadable 28-item allergen chart covering the set menu served at every branch, which is a real asset — but read it carefully before relying on it. On that chart the wheat (小麦) row is marked ー (not used) for the mains it lists, including the fried chicken and the chicken nanban, while soy (大豆) is marked 〇 across nearly all of them. Since Japanese soy sauce is a wheat product by default and the company nowhere names a gluten-free tamari, that pattern most likely means the chart is counting soy sauce as soy only, not that the kitchen is wheat-free. The chart also states in its own words that ingredients outside the 28 items and everything on each branch's own menu (小鉢, seasonal sets, evening dishes, chef's specials) must be asked about in store. So: ask, with a printed chart in hand, and confirm the soy sauce specifically. Karaage and chicken nanban are deep-fried in a shared fryer in any case.
vegan_detail: The format is fish or meat plus rice, miso soup and small dishes; the allergen chart's mains are all animal (nikujaga, simmered mackerel, chicken, hokke, tororo, mentaiko, nattō, raw egg). The clay-pot rice itself is plain rice and the pickles and nattō sides are plant-based, but the miso soup will be a bonito or niboshi dashi unless stated otherwise and nothing vegan is advertised. Assembling a vegan meal here means eating rice, nattō and pickles.

roles: 代表取締役 — president, 株式会社四季の台所
chef_bio.origin: Ebisu, Shibuya-ku — the company was founded there and still centres on it
chef_bio.background: Shiki no Daidokoro ('the kitchen of the four seasons') has been trading in Ebisu for close to forty years and now runs eleven-odd branches of 恵比寿 土鍋炊ごはん なかよし across Ebisu, Shibuya, Meguro, Yūrakuchō, Suidōbashi, Musashi-Kosugi and this Marunouchi basement, plus a 和定食 counter inside Gransta Tokyo that opened in April. The president Masaru Sunouchi signs a greeting on the company site that reads as a manifesto for a very specific idea of a set-meal shop: rice cooked in a donabe clay pot, refills free, no chemical seasonings, the menu changed every month, and — the line that stands out — 「どなたにもレシピを公開しています」, the recipes are published to anyone who asks. He frames the company's ambition as being a 街の食堂, the neighbourhood canteen, and argues that raising how people eat is not only about ingredients but about the room, the price balance, the staff, the sense of season and colour on the tray. The closing line of the greeting is 「人生は定食で変えられる。なんて、ちょっと言い過ぎかもしれません」 — life can be changed by a set meal; all right, perhaps that is going too far. No individual chef is credited for the Marunouchi branch; the company advertises openly for 料理長候補, kitchen-chief candidates, and runs the menu centrally.
chef_bio.philosophy: The neighbourhood canteen: donabe rice with free refills, no chemical seasonings, a menu that turns over monthly, and published recipes.
chef_bio.specialty: Clay-pot rice cooked to order, with a monthly teishoku line-up around it; seasonal 1.5-gō donabe of rice at night.

anecdotes.text: The company publishes its recipes to anyone who asks — 「どなたにもレシピを公開しています」 — which is close to unheard of for a restaurant group.
It also publishes a downloadable 28-item allergen chart for the set menu across all branches, with an explicit note that anything outside those 28 items must be asked about in store.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: shikinodaidokoro.co.jp's branch page gives 東京都千代田区丸の内1-4-1 丸の内永楽ビルB1F, phone 03-6812-2150, hours 11:00–23:00 (food L.O. 22:00, drink 22:30), Saturday 11:00–14:30, closed Sundays and public holidays, and states reservations must be made by phoning the branch directly. The company top page carries the president's signed greeting, the near-40-year Ebisu history, the eleven-branch count and the no-chemical-seasoning and free-refill claims. The /allergies page hosts the 28-item PDF. Tabelog (13272524) and Hot Pepper corroborate the address and add 大手町駅から85m; Marunouchi.com lists it as a Marunouchi Eiraku Building tenant.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Karaage and chicken nanban are on the standing set menu, so a fryer is running; nothing published suggests it is separated from anything else.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The published chart marks 大豆 (soy) for almost every main but 小麦 (wheat) for none, and the company never names a gluten-free tamari. The most likely reading is that soy sauce is being counted under soy alone — assume wheat soy sauce and confirm at the counter.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Every main on the chart is fish or meat, and the miso soup dashi is not specified.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The chart itself instructs guests to ask each branch about the other 28-item exclusions and about branch-original dishes — an explicit invitation to raise an allergy at the counter rather than a brush-off.

positives.text: A printable 28-item allergen chart covering the standard set menu at every branch, plus a company that publishes its recipes on request — far more transparency than a teishoku shop at this price usually offers.

cultural_comfort.note: An office-district basement canteen: cheap, fast, no reservation needed at lunch, tables rather than a counter, and a menu that is largely pointable. Closed Sundays and holidays and Saturday afternoons, which catches tourists out — this is a weekday-lunch room. Reservations for groups are by phone to the branch only (03-6812-2150); there is no online booking on the company site, though Hot Pepper takes them. No English menu is advertised.

enrich_note: Confirmed. The light record read 「土鍋炊ごはん なかよし 丸の内iiyo店」; the operator writes it 恵比寿 土鍋炊ごはん なかよし 丸の内iiyo!!店, which is the same shop — expanded rather than corrected. The light record's neighbourhood label 大手町 is right — Ōtemachi is the nearer station at 85 m. Downloaded and read the company's 28-item allergen PDF; its wheat row and its soy row disagree in a way that matters to a celiac, and that is written up in gf_detail rather than smoothed over. GF left at 'ask'.

name: 入金 (いりきん)
reopens: Relocating. Last day at Nihonbashi is Friday 28 August 2026; the shop reopens at 〒104-0031 東京都中央区京橋1-6-8 コルマ京橋ビル1F, which the owners planned for December 2026–January 2027.
address_ja: 〒103-0027 東京都中央区日本橋1-18-12（2026年8月28日まで）／移転先：〒104-0031 東京都中央区京橋1-6-8 コルマ京橋ビル1F
cuisine: A 1947 Nihonbashi shokudō that turns izakaya at night: fish-forward teishoku — the signature maguro-katsu (breaded tuna cutlet) set, sashimi sets, simmered tuna collar, grilled gindara saikyō-yaki at ¥1,140, kisu fry — with a big block of chilled tofu and side dishes you pick yourself; lunch runs about ¥650–¥1,100, dinner ¥2,000–¥3,000
neighborhood: Nihonbashi 1-chōme, down the alley beside the Nihonbashi post office off Shōwa-dōri — 3–4 min from Nihonbashi station (Tokyo Metro Ginza and Tōzai lines, exit D2), 245 m from the station, 8 min from Kayabachō
gf_detail: The house signature is maguro-katsu — tuna crumbed in panko and deep-fried — and the kisu fry and other fried sets come out of the same oil, so the fryer runs wheat all day. Teishoku seasoning here is ordinary Japanese soy sauce and miso; no gluten-free tamari is claimed anywhere, no allergen sheet is published, and the shop has no website. The saikyō-yaki uses Kyoto white miso, which is a rice miso rather than a barley one, but that is inference from the dish name, not a statement by the shop. Nothing here is set up for a celiac.
vegan_detail: A fish shokudō: tuna, mackerel, sea bream, gindara, kisu, sashimi. The soup will be a bonito or niboshi dashi. The chilled tofu that comes with the sets is the only substantial plant dish and it arrives with soy sauce and bonito flakes as standard. No vegan option is offered or advertised.

roles: 株式会社入金 — family-run since 1947
chef_bio.background: Irikin has been feeding Nihonbashi office workers since 1947 — its own X account describes the business as being in its 78th year — from an unremarkable building down an alley beside the Nihonbashi post office, off Shōwa-dōri, which reviewers repeatedly say they walked past before finding. Reviewers file it under 昭和遺産, a Shōwa relic: 40-odd seats at plain tables, cash only, no cards, no e-money, no QR payment, no website, a phone number and a signboard. The draw is fish bought properly and priced like a canteen — the house dish is maguro-katsu, tuna crumbed and fried, served as a set with a large block of chilled tofu and extra side dishes the customer chooses; sashimi sets and grilled fish sets rotate with what came in. Tabelog files it as both 食堂 and 居酒屋 because it is both: teishoku from 11:00, sake and shōchū and 魚料理にこだわる cooking from 17:00. In August 2026 the shop was caught by the large Nihonbashi 1-chōme redevelopment. It announced on 12 August that Friday 28 August would be its last day at the old address, and that it would reopen at 京橋1-6-8, on Kyōbashi's Kottō-dōri antique street, with an opening planned for December 2026 or January 2027 — a regular of thirteen visits went for a last lunch of gindara saikyō-yaki and titled the review 「次回は京橋で・・・」, next time in Kyōbashi.
chef_bio.specialty: まぐろカツ定食 — the tuna cutlet set — plus sashimi sets, tuna collar simmered in soy, and grilled fish of the day.

anecdotes.text: The shop is hard to find on purpose or by accident: it sits down an alley beside the Nihonbashi post office off Shōwa-dōri, and TripAdvisor reviewers warn that it is easy to walk straight past.
Cash only — no credit cards, no electronic money, no QR payment — in the middle of one of Tokyo's most corporate districts.
Its last Nihonbashi service is 28 August 2026, after 78 years, because the block is being redeveloped; the family is moving to Kyōbashi's antique street rather than closing.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog (13058389) gives 東京都中央区日本橋1-18-12, phone 03-3271-3694, hours 11:00–14:00 and 17:00–21:00 daily, 42 table seats, all non-smoking, cards/e-money/QR all unavailable, and a 3.46 rating over 142 reviews. gnavi (gk9026yt0000) agrees on the address and puts the lunch average at ¥650 and the overall average at ¥800; Mapion lists the same phone and address. Another review dates the founding to 1947.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The signature dish is panko-fried tuna and the menu carries other fry sets; one fryer serves all of them.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No allergen information is published and the shop has no website. Assume ordinary wheat soy sauce throughout — in the simmered dishes, on the chilled tofu and on the sashimi.

vegan_cross_contact.text: A fish kitchen from open to close; the soup is dashi and the tofu is served with bonito flakes.

cultural_comfort.note: A working-lunch shokudō with no website, no English menu, no cards and no e-money — bring cash and be ready to order from a Japanese board. It is easy to walk into (42 table seats, all non-smoking, reservations accepted on 03-3271-3694) and the crowd is local office workers, so the peak is 12:00–13:00 on weekdays. Most important practical point: check where it is before going. The Nihonbashi room closes for good on 28 August 2026 and the shop moves to Kyōbashi 1-6-8, with the reopening pencilled in for December 2026–January 2027.

name: 六厘舎 東京ラーメンストリート店
address_ja: 〒100-0005 東京都千代田区丸の内1-9-1 東京駅一番街B1F 東京ラーメンストリート内
cuisine: The tsukemen shop that made ultra-thick fish-and-pork dipping broth a national style — very fat noodles from Asakusa Kaikarō served cold beside a broth so reduced it coats the noodle, a raft of nori heaped with fish powder, and a yuzu-scented soup-thinner (スープ割) to finish; also a lighter chūka soba, and a morning-only 朝つけめん from 7:30, sold nowhere else
neighborhood: Tokyo Ramen Street on B1 of Tokyo Station Ichibangai, on the Yaesu side of Tokyo Station — inside the station complex, straight down from the Yaesu underground central exit
gf_detail: Ruled out by the company's own allergen table, dated 5 August 2026, which marks 小麦 (wheat) on every tsukemen, every chūka soba and every ramen it sells, and on the gyōza, the chāshū, the extra-broth and the take-home packs. Even the スープ割 finishing broth carries allergen marks. That is exactly what you would expect — the noodles are wheat and the tare is soy sauce — but it is good that they say so. The same sheet also states plainly that cooking utensils and dishes are not separated by product and that secondary contamination cannot be prevented. There is no gluten-free item here and no way to eat around it.
vegan_detail: The broth is a long-boiled pork-and-fish reduction and the fish powder on the nori is the house signature; chāshū, minced pork, egg and gyōza fill out the menu. The only animal-free lines on the allergen sheet are the spring-onion top-up, the spinach and the pickled ginger on the table. Nothing vegan is offered.

roles: brand now operated by 株式会社松富士食品 (Matsufuji Foods), president 竹田和重
Matsufuji acquired by Matsuya Foods Holdings
chef_bio.origin: Ōsaki, Shinagawa-ku, Tokyo — the original shop
chef_bio.background: Ryōsei Mita opened the first Rokurinsha in Ōsaki in April 2005 and very nearly failed: for the first months almost nobody came, and in what the shop treats as its founding decision he abandoned the safe recipe for the one he actually wanted — a hugely reduced broth against extremely thick noodles. It worked to a degree that became its own problem. Rokurinsha took the tsukemen prize in TOKYO 1-shūkan's Ramen of the Year in both 2006 and 2007, queues regularly passed a hundred people, and a two-hour wait was normal, two and a half hours over a long weekend. The Ōsaki shop finally closed on 29 August 2010 — not for lack of business but because the queue had become a lasting nuisance to the neighbours and there was no prospect of fixing it; the company said it would choose the next site carefully so as not to inconvenience anyone nearby. By then the Tokyo Station branch was already open: 六厘舎TOKYO started on Tokyo Ramen Street on 17 June 2009, and it is the branch that carried the name through. The technique is deliberately unglamorous — no luxury ingredients, just enormous quantities of ordinary ones boiled for a very long time and then crushed by hand until the solids disappear into the liquid. The noodles are not made in-house: they are cut to order by Asakusa Kaikarō after repeated trials, with the shop closing to hold recipe meetings with the noodle-maker. Rokurinsha is also the shop that started the now-copied habit of laying a raft of nori across the bowl and heaping powdered fish on it, so the diner stirs the fish in themselves. The brand today runs five Tokyo shops under Matsufuji Foods, which also owns Sharin, Junk Garage, Tonari and Jinenjo, and which Matsuya Foods Holdings bought for ¥9.1bn.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「つけめんを文化に」 — make tsukemen a culture. The company also states the dipping broth has been altered continuously since opening, deliberately by amounts small enough that regulars would not notice.
chef_bio.specialty: 特製つけめん and 生七味つけめん (a fresh seven-spice paste built from ten ingredients, aimed at aroma rather than heat); the Tokyo Station branch alone sells 特製朝つけめん before 9:30.

anecdotes.text: The original Ōsaki shop was closed on 29 August 2010 because its own queue — routinely 100 people, two hours, two and a half on holidays — had become an unfixable nuisance to the neighbourhood.
The noodles come from Asakusa Kaikarō, arrived at through repeated trials for which the shop shut to hold meetings with the noodle-maker.
This branch is the only one that sells the morning tsukemen, served 7:30–9:30 to people passing through the station.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The operator's official store page (shop.mtfj.co.jp/stores/61) gives 〒100-0005 東京都千代田区丸の内1-9-1 東京駅一番街B1F 東京ラーメンストリート内, phone 03-3286-0166, 26 seats, hours 7:30–9:45 and 10:00–23:00 every day, cash / transit IC / QR payment, takeout available. Tokyo Station Ichibangai's own shop guide repeats the hours and the two-part service and notes the morning-only 朝つけ. rokurinsha.com carries the brand statement and the full menu, and hosts a dated (2026-08-05) PDF allergen table. Japanese Wikipedia gives the 2005 Ōsaki founding by 三田遼斉, the 2006–2007 awards, the 29 August 2010 closure over queue complaints, the 17 June 2009 Tokyo Station opening, the Asakusa Kaikarō noodle sourcing and the Matsuya Foods ownership; Nikkei reported the ¥9.1bn acquisition of Matsufuji.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The company's allergen sheet states outright: 「当店で使用している調理器具・食器は商品ごとに使い分けをしておりません」 — utensils and dishes are not separated by product, and secondary contamination cannot be entirely prevented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Wheat is marked on every noodle dish and on the toppings and take-home packs; nothing on the sheet is free of it except plain vegetable toppings.

vegan_cross_contact.text: A pork-and-fish broth reduced over hours, finished with powdered fish; the only animal-free lines are negi, spinach and table pickled ginger.

staff_allergy_handling.text: A dated 28-item allergen table is published as a downloadable PDF and refreshed — the copy read here is dated 5 August 2026 — with an honest disclaimer that it cannot guarantee no reaction and that final judgement should be made with a specialist.

positives.text: The sheet also notes the noodles contain no egg, and that nori is farmed in waters where shrimp and crab occur — a level of detail most ramen shops never publish.

cultural_comfort.note: Inside the station, open 7:30 to 23:00 every day including holidays, 26 seats, ticket-machine style ordering and an English site (rokurinsha.com/en). Cash, transit IC cards and QR payment are all accepted; credit cards are not listed. Expect a queue — this is one of the most-visited ramen counters in Japan and Tokyo Ramen Street is on every station guide. Takeout and souvenir packs are sold, which is the easy way out if the line is long.

name: 四国 88屋 丸の内本店 (はちはちや)
address_ja: 〒100-0005 東京都千代田区丸の内1-4-1 丸の内永楽ビルディング iiyo!!（イーヨ!!） B1F
cuisine: A Shikoku regional izakaya in the iiyo!! basement, run by a tourism company from Imabari: bonito seared over a flare of burning rice straw in the dining room (土佐 本鰹の藁焼きタタキ), the same treatment given to Ainan gold yellowtail and to Tokushima's Mitsuboshi beef, plus Ehime sea bream, Imabari senzanki fried chicken, Uwajima taimeshi, Kagawa green-tea udon and Handa sōmen; about ¥1,300 at lunch, ¥5,500 a head at night, party courses with two hours of drinks from ¥5,500
neighborhood: Marunouchi 1-4-1, B1F of the Marunouchi Eiraku Building (iiyo!!) — 1 min from Ōtemachi station exit B1, directly connected underground; 5 min from Tokyo Station's Marunouchi north exit via the underground passage
gf_detail: No gluten-free claim and no allergen sheet published, so this is an ask — but it is an ask with a real answer, unlike most izakaya. The house dish is straw-seared tataki, and the menu itself tells you it is served 「お好みで『塩』または『ポン酢』で」 — with salt or with ponzu, your choice. Salt-seared bonito, the Kōchi 塩タタキ style, is naturally wheat-free; ponzu is not, because it is built on soy sauce. Salt-grilled fish collar (カマ塩焼き) is on the menu the same way. Against that: sashimi arrives with wheat soy sauce, the Kagawa green-tea udon and the Tokushima Handa sōmen are wheat noodles, and senzanki fried chicken, fried octopus, fried scabbardfish and olive-herb-salt potato fries all share one fryer. Order salt, skip the noodles and the fried plates, and say 小麦アレルギー clearly — the shop has English-speaking staff and an English menu, which makes that conversation easier than usual.
vegan_detail: This is a fish-and-meat house: straw-grilled bonito, yellowtail, sea bream, beef, fried chicken. Plant dishes exist as sides — Shōdoshima olive-herb-salt potato fries (shared fryer), Shikoku vegetables, the green-tea udon and Handa sōmen if the tsuyu can be left off, citrus drinks and local sake — but there is no vegan set and the noodle dipping sauces will be bonito-based. Possible to graze, not to eat a meal.

roles: 代表取締役社長 — president, 株式会社瀬戸内しまなみリーディング
chef_bio.origin: Imabari, Ehime — the company is headquartered at 今治市東鳥生町5-15
chef_bio.background: 88屋 is not a restaurant group's project; it is a regional development company's shop window in Tokyo. Setouchi Shimanami Leading was set up in Imabari in November 1996 with the stated mission of getting more people to the Shimanami Kaidō region, and its business list is unusual for a company that runs an izakaya in Marunouchi: the Shimanami Kaidō express bus service, the toll gates, road maintenance, the Kurushima Kaikyō service area, the Fukubu shokudō, an udon shop called Hachijūhachi Udon, a university canteen, Japan-Heritage tourism including a landing cruise to the pirate island of Noshima, regional product development — and the two Tokyo 88屋 branches, which the company describes plainly as a 拠点 for broadcasting the appeal of the Shimanami region. It employs 245 people across Imabari, Saijō and Tokyo under president Keiji Miyamoto. The Marunouchi shop opened as the honten and carries four separate prefectural endorsements — 愛媛県 食の大使館 (Ehime's 'embassy of food'), 徳島県 阿波ふうど, 高知県 高知家ぐるめナビ in 首都圏 and 香川県 首都圏かがわグルメガイド — which is to say all four Shikoku prefectures have signed off on it as their representative in Tokyo. A second branch opened at Ōtemachi in December 2025. The kitchen's set piece is done in the room: bonito shipped from Kōchi is seared in a blaze of burning rice straw, high heat and fast, so the outside chars and the inside stays raw, and the diner is told to eat it with salt or ponzu as they prefer. Fish comes direct — the yellowtail from Ainan-chō in Ehime, the sea bream wild-caught from Ehime, the beef Tokushima's Mitsuboshi brand, down to a rare cut called tōgarashi, and the sōmen from Handa in Tsurugi-chō, where it has been made for about 270 years and is cut noticeably thicker than ordinary sōmen.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「しまなみ地域の魅力をより多くの人に伝え、訪問者を増やし、地域全体を元気にして、ともに発展すること」 — tell more people about the Shimanami region, bring visitors, and grow with the place.
chef_bio.specialty: 本鰹の藁焼きタタキ — bonito seared over burning straw in front of the room — and the 豪快88屋盛り, two straw-grilled fish plus three sashimi from that morning's market.

anecdotes.text: The operator's other lines of business include running the Shimanami Kaidō's express buses, its toll gates and its service area; the Marunouchi izakaya is the Tokyo end of a regional tourism company.
All four Shikoku prefectures certify the shop — Ehime's 食の大使館, Tokushima's 阿波ふうど, Kōchi's 高知家ぐるめナビ and Kagawa's 首都圏かがわグルメガイド.
The Handa sōmen on the menu comes from Tsurugi-chō in western Tokushima, where it has been made for roughly 270 years and is deliberately thicker than standard sōmen.

name: 天ぷら日本酒 天喜代 東京駅店
address_ja: 〒100-0005 東京都千代田区丸の内1-9-1 グランルーフB1（グランスタ八重洲内）
cuisine: A tempura-and-sake counter inside the station, run by the 1927 Shimotakaido sushi house Asahizushi — seasonal seafood and vegetables fried in a safflower-oil blend in an open kitchen, with dishes you will not find at a normal tempura shop: sea urchin wrapped in nori and fried, whole Kujūkuri clams fried in the shell, and a sake list chosen dish by dish; about ¥1,000–¥1,500 at lunch, ¥2,000–¥3,000 at night, banquet courses ¥7,000–¥8,000 with two hours of drinks
neighborhood: Marunouchi 1-9-1, B1 of GranRoof inside the Gransta Yaesu concourse — through the JR Yaesu underground central exit, past Tokyo Okashi Land and right at Sushisei in front of Daimaru; 3 min from JR Tokyo Station, 5 min from the Marunouchi subway line
hours_raw: 月～日・祝日・祝前日 11:00～22:00（料理L.O.21:00／ドリンクL.O.21:00）　グランスタ八重洲に準ずる　定休日：無
gf_detail: A tempura specialist with an open kitchen and one fryer. Everything is wheat batter, including the two house signatures (uni wrapped in nori, whole clam in the shell), and the tentsuyu is wheat soy sauce. The oil is a safflower blend — the light record was right about that, and the operator says so in its own listings — but safflower oil is a lightness claim, not an allergen one. No gluten-free item, no allergen sheet, no separate fryer. The sake list is a further reason for care: most junmai is fine, but the shop makes no statement about it.
vegan_detail: Built on the parent company's sushi buying: prawns, seasonal fish, sea urchin, clams. Vegetable tempura exists inside the courses but shares the fryer with seafood and the dipping sauce is a bonito tentsuyu. Nothing vegan is offered.

roles: a tempura brand of 旭鮨總本店株式会社 (Asahizushi Sōhonten Co., Ltd.), 下高井戸
chef_bio.origin: Shimotakaido, Setagaya-ku — the parent company's first shop, on the Keiō line
chef_bio.background: Tenkiyo is the tempura arm of a Setagaya sushi company whose own history is better than most standalone restaurants'. The founder, Kanjirō Takano, was a tabi craftsman who went independent in 1916 and hung out a sign reading 旭屋; on 1 February 1927 he opened a soba shop called Asahiya beside Shimotakaido station on the Keiō line, and that is the date the company counts as its founding. The character 旭 was chosen over the ordinary 朝日 for a reason the company still explains on its site: 旭 breaks apart into 九日, nine days — one short of ten, one short of completion — as a standing reminder never to feel finished. The Pacific War killed the business; Asahiya was forced to close in 1944. It came back in 1949, under the postwar law reopening food and drink premises, as 旭鮨 doing 鮨委託加工 — commissioned sushi processing — because rice was still controlled: a customer handed over a gō of rice, the shop turned it into sushi for a fee of 60 yen, and since eating on the premises was forbidden the whole trade was delivery, with the rice collected when the dishes were fetched back. Controls lifted in 1950, the firm incorporated in 1952, put a counter into the Keiō department store food hall in Shinjuku in 1964, and renamed itself Asahizushi Sōhonten in 1968. It now runs about twenty shops around Tokyo — sushi, fugu, tempura and Japanese cooking — with 90 permanent and 216 part-time staff and turnover around ¥2bn, and it reaches its centenary in 2027. Its own line about that is 「まだまだ100年です」 — a hundred years is still not much. Tenkiyo is the tempura format, at Tokyo Station and at Fujisawa, and the pitch is specific: because a sushi company is doing the buying, the fish on the counter is not what a tempura shop would normally get, and the sake is chosen against the individual dish rather than as a list. The frying is done in front of the room in an open kitchen; the shop's own description leans on the sound and smell of it as part of the meal.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「お客様に喜びを」 — give the customer joy; and the founder's 旭, the character that means one day short of completion.
chef_bio.specialty: うに磯辺天婦羅 (sea urchin in nori, fried), 蛤姿揚げ (whole Kujūkuri clam fried in the shell), and tempura courses matched to sake — the ¥7,000 Kaze course and the ¥8,000 Sora course.

anecdotes.text: The company name is a private instruction. 旭 was picked instead of 朝日 because it decomposes into 九日 — nine days out of ten — so that the family would never feel the job was done.

In 1949 the shop could not legally serve food on the premises. Customers brought a gō of rice, the shop turned it into sushi for 60 yen, and the rice was collected when the delivery dishes were picked up.
The Shimotakaido main shop is currently being rebuilt, and the company reached its 99th year in February 2026 — the centenary falls in 2027.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The branch's own site (tenkiyo-tokyo.owst.jp) gives 東京都千代田区丸の内1-9-1 グランルーフB1, phone 03-6269-9926, 11:00–22:00 daily with no closing day, 33 seats (8 counter, 25 table), all non-smoking, barrier-free, cards and every major e-money and QR wallet accepted, the ¥1,001–1,500 lunch and ¥2,001–3,000 dinner averages, the cancellation terms, walking directions from the Yaesu underground central exit, and menus in English, Korean and both Chinese scripts. It states plainly that the shop is run by 旭鮨総本店. Tabelog (13160654) and gnavi confirm the address; the Fujisawa sister branch's listings state that the tempura is fried in a safflower blend (紅花ブレンドの油). asahizushi.com carries the company chronology from 1916 and the corporate profile: founded 1 February 1927, incorporated 13 March 1952, capital ¥45m, turnover about ¥2bn in FY2024, 20 shops, head office in Akatsutsumi, Setagaya-ku.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen's stated advantage is that a sushi company buys its fish; sea urchin, clams and seasonal seafood run through the same oil as the vegetables.

positives.text: Menus in English, Korean, simplified and traditional Chinese, so ingredients can at least be read before ordering.
Counter seating at an open kitchen — you can watch what goes into the oil.

cultural_comfort.note: Inside Tokyo Station, open 11:00–22:00 every day with no closing day, barrier-free, all seats non-smoking, and menus in five languages. Credit cards, Suica and PASMO, and the Chinese QR wallets are all accepted. 33 seats, 8 of them at the counter; online booking through Hot Pepper or gnavi, or phone 03-6269-9926. Note the cancellation terms — a course booking incurs 50% after 22:00 the night before, and a seat-only booking ¥1,000 after 15:00 on the day. Takeout is available if the counter is full.

name: 竹末東京Premium
address_ja: 〒130-0002 東京都墨田区業平5-14-7 フラーリシ押上 1F
cuisine: A twelve-seat ramen counter under the Skytree that cooks each bowl in front of you — silky chicken paitan from birds killed to order under direct farm contract, the house 鶏ホタテそば finished with scallop, plus shōyu and shio soba, a chicken tsukemen and irregular one-day limited bowls; ¥1,000–¥1,999 a head, cash or card
neighborhood: Narihira 5-chōme, Sumida-ku — about 10 minutes east of Oshiage station along the road south of Tokyo Skytree (Toei Asakusa, Hanzōmon, Keisei Oshiage and Tobu Skytree lines); 35 m from Jikkenbashi bridge. This is NOT Marunouchi
hours_raw: 11:00～15:00（料理L.O.14:45）／17:00～21:00（料理L.O.20:45）　火曜定休（祝日は営業）※突発の休業や限定麺は公式X（@takesuetokyo）で告知　予約不可
gf_detail: Wheat noodles and a soy-sauce tare — the shōyu soba is the house's oldest bowl and even the shio and paitan bowls are seasoned with soy-based tare unless the shop says otherwise, which it does not. One of its signature bowls is a jirō-style built on Kanno Seimen thick wheat noodles, and a food-media write-up of it explicitly describes the wheat aroma as part of the dish. No allergen information is published, the shop has no working website, and twelve seats and one pot mean nothing can be separated. Not a possibility for a celiac.
vegan_detail: The entire premise is chicken — whole birds boiled down for the paitan, the chicken fat emulsified into it, contracted farms slaughtering after the order goes in — plus scallop, mackerel-pike and squid on the seasonal bowls, chāshū, egg and a meat-and-egg rice bowl. There is no vegetable bowl and no plant-based broth.

roles: 店主 — owner-chef since taking the shop over independently in 2020
chef_bio.origin: Oshiage, Sumida-ku; the parent shop is 竹末 in Sakura, Tochigi
chef_bio.background: Takesue Tokyo Premium opened on 30 April 2014 as the Tokyo outpost of a well-known Tochigi shop, ラーメン専門店 E.Y竹末, and traded on that reputation from its first day. In 2020, six years in, the manager Tsubasa Ōe took it over as his own — 独立継承, an independent succession rather than a franchise renewal — and it is his kitchen now. The house term for what happens at the counter is RAMEN LIVE TUNE: rather than assembling bowls out of sight, every bowl is finished in front of the twelve seats, which the shop cheerfully admits is an operation that breaks the normal rules of ramen service. The sourcing is the other half of it. Everything is domestic, and the chicken is bought on direct contract with farms that begin the process only once the order has gone in, so the birds arrive unusually fresh; the fat emulsifies into a paitan the trade press describes as closer to a potage — creamy and silky, but finishing light enough to drink the bowl dry. Ōe's stated rule is that he will not make ramen that sits heavy on the stomach, and the shop's most famous bowl, the 鶏ホタテそば, is chicken paitan lifted with scallop. It has been named to Tabelog's Ramen Hyakumeiten every year from 2017 to 2023 — seven consecutive years, which the shop's own X profile leads with — and holds a 3.77 rating over more than 2,000 reviews. Limited bowls appear without warning on anniversaries or on a whim, and closures are announced only on X, so regulars check the account before travelling.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「RAMEN LIVE TUNE」 — the bowl built in front of the guest as performance; and a refusal to make ramen that leaves you heavy.
chef_bio.specialty: 鶏ホタテそば — chicken paitan with scallop — plus 醤油そば, 塩そば and a chicken tsukemen; occasional trout and seasonal-fish bowls.

anecdotes.text: The chicken is contracted directly with farms which only slaughter after the order is placed, which is why the paitan behaves like a potage.
Twelve seats, no reservations, and cushions laid out on the pavement outside for the queue.
Ōe took the shop over from the Tochigi parent as his own in 2020, six years after it opened, and it has been on Tabelog's ramen top-100 list every year from 2017 to 2023.

name: つじ田 日本橋八重洲店
address_ja: 〒103-0028 東京都中央区八重洲1-4-6 八重洲境井ビル 1F
cuisine: A sixteen-seat counter for 濃厚豚骨魚介つけ麺 — thick pork-bone-and-seafood dipping broth with chewy custom noodles, eaten to a house ritual: plain first, a squeezed sudachi at the one-third mark, Kyoto black shichimi over the last third, then a soup-wari to finish; ¥1,100 for the plain tsukemen with ajitama, tokusei and pork-crumble versions above it, the same broth also served as ramen, rice bowls alongside, ¥1,000–¥1,999 a head
neighborhood: Yaesu 1-chōme, Chūō-ku — 263 m and 1–3 min on foot from Nihonbashi station exit A7 (Tokyo Metro Tōzai and Ginza lines), or 5 min from the JR Tokyo Station Yaesu north exit. Not the Nihonbashi-bridge block the light record pinned
hours_raw: 平日：11:00～22:30／土日祝：11:00〜21:30（公式店舗ページ。お知らせ欄に「祝日の営業時間は11:00～21:30です」）　定休日：不定休　※食べログ・ぐるなびは土・日・祝を11:00～21:00と記載しており、公式と30分ずれる
gf_detail: Ruled out by the operator's own published allergen statement, not by inference. オイシーズ株式会社, which runs つじ田, states 「当店の厨房設備及び商品の製造上、アレルギー食材を完全に除くことができません」, that every menu item is cooked with the same equipment so ingredients not belonging to a dish can transfer into it, and — decisively — 「麺、スープ等の製造工場では、小麦、卵、乳成分を原材料とする商品の製造を行ってます」. It adds that guests who react to trace amounts may be refused service. The product itself is wheat regardless: two custom wheat noodles co-developed with 三河屋製麺, and a tonkotsu-gyokai tare with no gluten-free tamari named anywhere. One noodle pot serves sixteen seats.
vegan_detail: The whole brand is built on a pork-bone and seafood dipping broth; the standard bowl carries chāshū and the popular version adds a marinated soft-boiled egg, with a 豚崩し pork-crumble variant above it and chāshū rice, takana rice and a 替え飯 as the sides. There is no vegetable broth and no plant-based dipping sauce, and the operator's allergen page confirms egg and dairy are handled on the same production line as the noodles and soup.

roles: Brand of オイシーズ株式会社 (OISHES Co., Ltd.), 東京都千代田区神田神保町3-2 高橋ビルディング5階 — the operator publishes no individual chef or founder name for this branch
chef_bio.origin: Kanda-Ochanomizu, Chiyoda-ku — where the first つじ田 opened in 2005
chef_bio.background: つじ田 is the shop usually credited with pushing 濃厚豚骨魚介つけ麺 out of the specialist scene and into Tokyo's business districts. Its own history page is brisk about it: 「2005年神田御茶ノ水でオープンして以来、味へ圧倒的なこだわりで東京のつけ麺文化を牽引」, expanding through Iidabashi and Yaesu into Osaka, Kanagawa, Saitama and Fukuoka, and opening in Los Angeles in 2011. The Yaesu branch is one of the older Tokyo outposts, trading since 10 July 2013 on the ground floor of the Yaesu Sakai building a minute from Nihonbashi station's A7 exit, and it is exactly what the chain is for — a lunchtime queue of office workers turning over sixteen counter seats. The kitchen publishes three things it will commit to. The soup is built from pork bone, chicken frame, seafood, kombu, vegetables and more than a dozen ingredients in total, with the shop stating openly that it will not disclose the sourcing: 「細かい産地、材料を公表することは出来ない」. The noodles are two bespoke wheat noodles — one for tsukemen, one for ramen — co-developed with 三河屋製麺, with a footnote that some regions are supplied by a different mill making the same つじ田-only spec. The condiment is Hara Ryōkaku's 黒七味 from Kyoto, a one-heir-per-generation blend made since 1704 that carried an Imperial Household warrant in the Meiji and Taishō eras; some branches substitute an in-house roasted black shichimi. The house rule for eating it, printed as つけ麺流儀, is four lines: eat it as it comes, squeeze sudachi over the noodles at the one-third mark and mix, dust the last third with black shichimi, then raise your soup bowl and ask staff for a soup-wari. Tabelog rates the branch 3.43 across 1,185 reviews with more than 26,000 saves.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「常においしさを求めて進化を続けること」 — the stated rule is to keep changing the recipe rather than freeze it, while holding the flavour.
chef_bio.specialty: 濃厚つけ麺 and its 味玉 / 特製 / 豚崩し variants, the same broth as 濃厚らーめん, and the つけ麺流儀 sudachi-and-black-shichimi ritual.

anecdotes.text: The black shichimi on the counter is 原了郭's, a Kyoto house founded in 1704 that has passed the recipe down one heir at a time and held an Imperial Household warrant; つじ田 uses it as the third stage of its prescribed way of eating a bowl.
The brand went to Los Angeles in 2011, six years after opening in Kanda-Ochanomizu, and now runs miso and tantanmen spin-off brands from the same company.
Sixteen counter seats, no reservations, ticket machine at the door; reviewers routinely record a wait at noon and a seat within a minute at nine at night.

gf_cross_contamination.text: 「当店の厨房設備及び商品の製造上、アレルギー食材を完全に除くことができません。各メニューの調理には同じ調理器具を使用しているため、本来その商品に使用しない食材が調理時に付着・混入する可能性があります。」 — the operator's own words. Sixteen seats, one noodle pot.
「麺、スープ等の製造工場では、小麦、卵、乳成分を原材料とする商品の製造を行ってます。」 The contamination risk starts upstream of the shop, in the factory.
「微量の原因物質でアレルギー症状を発症されるお客様には商品の提供をお断りさせていただく場合がございます。」 The company reserves the right to refuse service to trace-sensitive guests — the opposite of a guarantee.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth is finished with a tonkotsu-gyokai tare and the noodles are two custom wheat noodles made with 三河屋製麺. No gluten-free tamari and no wheat-free noodle is named anywhere on the brand site.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Pork bone and chicken frame are the base of every bowl; chāshū, ajitama and a pork-crumble bowl are on the board, and the factory line also runs egg and dairy.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The company does publish per-item allergen tables by brand, keyed to the 8 mandatory and 20 recommended Japanese allergen categories, and tells guests to re-check them every visit because recipes change. That is real transparency — but it is disclosure, not accommodation, and it is paired with the refusal-of-service clause.

cultural_comfort.note: A ticket-machine counter shop: buy a food ticket at the door, take one of sixteen counter seats, no reservations, no private rooms, all non-smoking. Cards and QR payment are not accepted — cash or a transit IC card such as Suica. Expect a queue at lunch and almost none late in the evening. Children are welcome, and takeout and Uber Eats delivery are both offered. The brand's four-step eating instructions (plain, then sudachi, then black shichimi, then ask for a スープ割り) are posted in Japanese and worth reading up on beforehand; asking for the soup-wari at the end is expected rather than pushy. Coeliacs should not eat here at all — the operator publishes that it may refuse service to trace-sensitive guests.

name: 京都銀閣寺 ますたに 日本橋本店
address_ja: 〒103-0027 東京都中央区日本橋2-10-3 エグゼトゥール日本橋 1F
cuisine: Kyoto 背脂チャッチャ ramen — a domestic chicken-bone shōyu broth capped with top-grade pork back fat and a heap of Kujō leek trucked down from Kyoto every morning, built deliberately in three layers (sweet and mild on top, clean soy in the middle, a chilli bite at the bottom) so the bowl changes as you drink it; ¥980 for the standard bowl, ¥1,230 for the chāshū version, ¥1,100 for the spicy miso, with a free bowl of rice and takuan thrown in with any noodle order
neighborhood: Nihonbashi 2-chōme, Chūō-ku — 133 m and about 3 min from Nihonbashi station exit C4 (Tokyo Metro Tōzai and Ginza lines, Toei Asakusa line), on the Shōwa-dōri side of Eitai-dōri
gf_detail: Wheat noodles in a soy-sauce broth, and the shop names the soy sauce as a point of pride — 「醤油 こだわりの徳島醤油」 — with no mention anywhere of a gluten-free tamari. Nothing on the site, the menu page or the news blog addresses allergens at all. The side board adds 九条ネギ焼餃子 (wheat gyōza skins) fried in the same kitchen, and the summer specials include a 魚介風煮干し醬油つけそば, i.e. more soy. Ordering is by ticket machine at a counter-led shop with no allergen sheet and no published wheat-free line; there is nothing here for a coeliac.
vegan_detail: The broth is 国産鶏がら — domestic chicken frames — finished with 国産極上背脂, pork back fat, which is the entire identity of the style. Chāshū (shoulder loin, 8–10 slices on the chāshū bowl) and eggs, both a marinated soft-boiled one and a raw one, are the standard toppings, and the free rice arrives with takuan. There is no vegetable broth and no meat-free bowl on the board.

roles: Official のれん分け (branch by blessing) of 京都ますたに総本店; the Nihonbashi operator runs two shops, 日本橋本店 and 日本橋室町店, and publishes no individual owner's name
chef_bio.origin: Kyoto — the parent shop stands near Ginkaku-ji in Sakyō-ku; this branch has traded in Nihonbashi, Chūō-ku, for decades
chef_bio.background: ますたに is one of the founding names of Kyoto ramen. Kyoto's official tourism site places it alongside 新福菜館 (1938) and 本家第一旭 in the city's founding generation and credits it specifically with creating 背脂チャッチャ系 — the technique of flicking rendered pork back fat over a soy broth at the moment of serving. This Nihonbashi shop is an official のれん分け from that house, and its own site leads with 「60年以上の歴史をもつ『京都ますたに総本店』からのれん分け」. What arrives is the Kyoto bowl rather than a Tokyo reinterpretation: the shop builds the soup in three deliberate layers and tells you so — the top sweet and mild from the back fat, the middle a clean soy, the bottom given a chilli bite — and advises drinking it straight from the bowl rather than with a renge, because the renge mixes the layers together. The sourcing list is short and specific: domestic chicken frames, Kujō leek shipped from Kyoto daily, shoulder-loin chāshū, Tokushima soy sauce, top-grade domestic back fat, first-pick nori, select rice, and eggs it calls こだわり卵. Rice is free with any noodle order, and in March 2025 the shop added a ¥300 upgrade that turns it into a 九条ネギ丼 with sesame oil, Korean nori flakes and shredded chāshū. The shop was pushed out of its long-standing address at 日本橋1-6-7 関谷ビル by redevelopment; on 3 September 2020 it announced the new site — 「現店舗より、徒歩1分！永代通りを渡った昭和通り沿い」, near the Nakau — and reopened at 日本橋2-10-3 in mid-November 2020, which is why a shop this old sits in a bright, new room. It remains one of the best-regarded ramen counters in the district, third in Tabelog's Nihonbashi ramen ranking at 3.59 over 1,182 reviews, and it is still posting seasonal menus in 2026: a 冷やしラーメン and a 魚介風煮干し醬油つけそば went up on 7 July 2026.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「一杯のラーメンに 真心 込めて」 — the line the shop leads its own site with.
chef_bio.specialty: 背脂鶏ガラ醤油ラーメン in the Kyoto style, three-layer soup, mounded Kujō leek; also 辛みそラーメン, つけそば, a weekend-and-holiday-only ますたにスペシャル, and summer-only 冷やしラーメン and 魚介風煮干し醬油つけそば.

anecdotes.text: The Kujō leek is sent from Kyoto every day — 「九条ネギ 京都より毎日直送」 — and the standard bowl can be ordered with a double heap of it for ¥150 more.
The shop asks you not to reach for the renge: drink straight from the bowl and the three layers of the soup arrive in sequence instead of blending into one.

Displaced by redevelopment, it announced its new address on 3 September 2020 with the reassurance that it was one minute away, across Eitai-dōri on Shōwa-dōri near the Nakau — and reopened that November.
Rice is free with any noodle order and you pick the portion; since March 2025, ¥300 converts it into a 九条ネギ丼 with sesame oil, Korean nori flakes and shredded chāshū.

cultural_comfort.note: Ticket machine at the entrance and cash only — Tabelog records no cards, no e-money and no QR payment, so bring notes. Counter-led with a few tables, open 10:30 to 22:30 almost every day of the year, no reservations, and the turnover is fast enough that reviewers report walking in without a wait outside peak lunch. A bowl of rice with takuan comes free with any noodle order and you choose the portion; the ticket machine's top-left button is the extra-Kujō-leek bowl at ¥1,130. Everything is in Japanese and no English menu is advertised, but ordering is a button press and the room is bright and modern (rebuilt in 2020), which makes it an easier first Japanese ramen counter than most. All non-smoking. The one date to avoid is the first Sunday of the month, when it closes at 15:00. Do not confuse it with the sister shop 日本橋室町店, ten minutes north.

name: 薮伊豆総本店
cuisine: An Edo soba house behind a gated wooden frontage, in the Yabu line since 1882 and still milling its own buckwheat twice a day in a stone-mill hut by the gate before cutting it 二八 by hand — seiro ¥650, 天せいろ ¥1,450, 上天せいろ ¥1,850, 鴨せいろ ¥1,650, the house 薮伊豆のごまそば ¥1,450, and a weekday じゅげむ定食 at ¥1,350 named after a rakugo routine; upstairs are 120 seats of tatami and horigotatsu rooms where sake and 蕎麦前 nibbles come before the noodles, banquet courses ¥5,500–¥8,800, and live rakugo three or four times a month
neighborhood: Nihonbashi 3-chōme, Chūō-ku, just off Shōwa-dōri — 4 min from Nihonbashi station exit D1 (Tokyo Metro Tōzai and Ginza lines, Toei Asakusa line), 6 min from Kayabachō exit 12 (Tōzai and Hibiya lines), 9 min from the JR Tokyo Station Yaesu central exit
hours_raw: 【ランチ】月～金曜日 11:15～14:00／土曜日・祝日 11:30～14:00　【ディナー】月～金曜日 17:15～20:15／土曜日・祝日 17:15～19:30　定休日：日曜日　8/11～8/15 夏季休業　※2026年9/21（月祝）～9/24（木）は設備改修のため休業、9/5（土）は昼のみ営業　※「従業員の福利厚生として」日曜定休以外に不定期の臨時休業あり
gf_detail: Wheat is designed into the noodle here, not merely nearby. The shop states plainly that it mills its own buckwheat and cuts it 二八 — 「自家製粉を二八で打ち」 — which is one part wheat flour to four parts buckwheat, and its mail-order soba is described as 「蕎麦粉50%以上の細打ちの江戸そば」, i.e. as little as half buckwheat. On top of that the tsuyu is a soy-sauce kaeshi over katsuobushi and saba-bushi dashi; tempura runs across the menu (天せいろ, 天ぷらそば, 天南蛮, いかの天ぷら, 季節の野菜の天ぷら) in wheat batter from a shared fryer; and hand-cut noodles mean dusting flour on the board and one shared boiling pot. No gluten-free claim, no tamari and no allergen sheet appear anywhere on the site. Per the brief's Japan rules this is precisely the case where a soba house reads as safe and is not.
vegan_detail: Every soba here is eaten with the house dashi, and the house dashi is the thing they are proudest of: 「出汁には、サバ節とカツオ節を6種類、独自の配合にて出汁を作り上げます」, drawn fresh each morning in a large kettle. That rules out the tsuyu, the kake bowls, the 揚げ浸し and the canned mail-order soup alike. There are genuinely good vegetable plates on the 蕎麦前 board — きゅうりとみょうがの甘酢漬け ¥600, ごまだれ豆腐 ¥750, ナスとピーマンの揚げ浸し ¥850, 季節の野菜の天ぷら ¥1,500 — but the age-bitashi sits in dashi, the tempura batter is egg-and-wheat and shares a fryer with prawn and squid, and the noodles themselves reach the table with a fish broth. No vegan option is published and none should be assumed.

chef_bio.chef_name: 野川喜央 (Nogawa) — 代表, 株式会社薮伊豆総本店
roles: 代表 (representative) of 株式会社薮伊豆総本店, named on the shop's own mail-order page
六代目当主 — the shop describes its present head as the sixth generation
女将 野川雅江 (Masae Nogawa) — the okami who runs the front of house and the rakugo programme
chef_bio.origin: Nihonbashi, Chūō-ku, by way of Kyōbashi; the okami, Masae Nogawa, is from Mori-machi in Shizuoka
chef_bio.background: The shop's own 薮伊豆由来記 traces the house to the Tempō years of the Edo period, around 1830, when a soba shop called 伊豆本 was already doing well in Kyōbashi. In 1882 — Meiji 15 — 伊豆本 was taken under the noren of 神田やぶそば, and 堀田定次郎 of the Yabu main house combined the 藪 of Yabu with the 伊豆 of Izumoto to make 薮伊豆, a direct branch of the Yabu lineage, one of the three great Edo soba schools. It moved from Kyōbashi to Nihonbashi in the late 1990s and the present head is the sixth generation; the 由来記 scroll itself hangs on the second floor. What separates it from the many old soba names in this district is that it still mills its own flour on site. Whole buckwheat is ground twice a day, morning and evening, in a stone-mill hut beside the gate, on 蟻巣石 millstones — porous, full of air pockets, heat-absorbing — turned slowly so the flour does not scorch and so the sweet inner husk goes into it. The flour is cut the same day, hand-kneaded, and the critical 水回し step is done in the technique handed down from Edo. The dashi is the other half: six kinds of saba-bushi and katsuobushi in a house ratio, boiled each morning in a large kettle with the scum skimmed off by hand and strained, following the old maxim 「出汁は大きく取れ」. The building runs to three floors and about 120 seats — a table floor at street level laid out deliberately for solo diners, tables plus a horigotatsu room on the second, and four tatami private rooms on the third whose fusuma can be removed to make a 40-seat hall. That third floor doubles as a rakugo theatre: the house holds a 落語会 three or four times a month, with a ¥2,500 「おアトもよろしくセット」 afterwards — tamagoyaki, itawasa, squid-and-vegetable tempura, kinpira, a simmered seasonal vegetable and two seiro. The connection is inherited rather than a marketing idea. Back when the shop was in Kyōbashi, the fifth-generation Yanagiya Kosan held his school's rakugo evenings in the third-floor tatami room alongside Reireisha Bafū and Shōkyokusai Sumie; the family stayed close to the Yanagiya school and Kosan's grandson, Yanagiya Karoku, now runs a 落語とそばの会 there. The lunch set is named 「じゅげむ定食」 after the rakugo piece Jugemu — chicken-and-burdock yanagawa hotpot, buckwheat-grain rice, kōya-dōfu, kinpira, kamaboko and soba, built around health and longevity, low in fat and heavy on fibre.
chef_bio.philosophy: 「そば本来の姿」を変えない — carry Edo townsmen's soba forward without altering what soba is; and soba as culture and 粋 rather than a way of filling up.
chef_bio.specialty: Self-milled stone-ground 二八 seiro, the house ごまそば, 鴨せいろ and 鴨南蛮, the じゅげむ定食 lunch, banquet courses in tatami private rooms, and the monthly rakugo evenings.

anecdotes.text: 「京橋に店があった頃、落語家の五代目柳家小さん師匠が店の3階のお座敷で、小さん一門による落語会をやっていました。それも、小さん、鈴々舎馬風、松旭斎すみゑ、と豪華でしたね」 — the okami, Masae Nogawa. Kosan's grandson Yanagiya Karoku now holds a 落語とそばの会 in the same room.
The lunch set is named after the rakugo routine Jugemu and themed on health and longevity: chicken-and-burdock yanagawa, buckwheat-grain rice, kōya-dōfu, kinpira, kamaboko and soba.

Buckwheat is stone-milled in a hut beside the gate twice a day and cut the same day; the millstones are 蟻巣石, chosen because their air pockets keep the flour from scorching and let the sweet inner husk through.

A Shizuoka prefectural feature on Shizuoka natives running Tokyo businesses profiles the okami, Masae Nogawa of Mori-machi, and records the shop's own line: 「明治15年に神田の藪から暖簾を分けられ『薮伊豆』となって、今の主人で6代目です」, with rakugo on the third floor three or four times a month.

Rakugo dates are posted as they are set — 8/22 Sangorō, 8/29 Yumemaru, 9/12 Tsukasa, 9/19 Sangorō, 9/20 Karoku (sold out), 9/26 Benzaitei Izumi, 10/5 Karoku, 10/10 Tsukasa, 10/24 Sangorō — and the shop links a PDF schedule from its own site.

The 店内のご案内 page describes the three floors and the hospital-grade air cleaners on the second. The 寄席 page gives the rakugo programme and the ¥2,500 「おアトもよろしくセット」. The お取り寄せ page names the operating company 株式会社薮伊豆総本店 and its 代表 野川喜央, and states that the mail-order soba is 蕎麦粉50%以上 and made under contract at a factory while the canned tsuyu is made in the shop's own kitchen over three days with no preservatives or additives. Tabelog (13006318) independently gives the same address and phone, 日本橋駅から358m, an オープン日 of 1882, 100 seats over three floors with private tatami rooms for 4 to 30-plus, cards accepted, all non-smoking, and 「定期落語会」 in its notes. Gnavi (gakp200) gives WGS84 coordinates 35.679039 / 139.775182, 120 seats, PayPay, wheelchair access, an English menu, banquet courses at ¥5,500 and ¥8,800, a ¥2,500 third-floor room charge, drink packages named after rakugo pieces, and a page last updated 17 August 2026. gf_cross_contamination.text: Hand-cut noodles on a dusted board, one boiling pot, and a fryer running prawn, squid and vegetable tempura for the same dining rooms. No separated line and no allergen sheet on any page of the shop's site.
The noodle itself is 二八 by the shop's own statement — 「自家製粉を二八で打ち」 — so wheat is an ingredient, not a contaminant. The mail-order version is 「蕎麦粉50%以上」, i.e. as little as half buckwheat.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The tsuyu is an ordinary soy-sauce kaeshi over the house katsuo/saba dashi. No tamari or wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned anywhere, and the canned tsuyu sold by mail order is the same recipe.

vegan_cross_contact.text: 「出汁には、サバ節とカツオ節を6種類、独自の配合にて出汁を作り上げます」 — bonito and mackerel dashi is the base of every tsuyu, every kake bowl and the 揚げ浸し. Tamagoyaki, kamaboko, duck and prawn run through the rest of the menu.

positives.text: Gnavi records an English menu and step-free wheelchair entry, and course bookings are taken online and through the shop's LINE account — so a dietary question can at least be put in writing before arrival, in a room that takes reservations. That is access, not an allergen guarantee.

cultural_comfort.note: Easier than it looks from the gate. There is an English menu, an English page on the shop's own site, step-free wheelchair entry, all major cards plus PayPay, and the ground floor is laid out deliberately for solo diners, so a walk-in lunch of one seiro needs no Japanese at all. The upstairs is where the effort pays: tatami and horigotatsu private rooms for 4 to 40, banquet courses from ¥5,500 (¥8,800 with two hours of premium sake), a ¥2,500 per-room charge on the third floor, and drink packages named after rakugo pieces — 時そば ¥2,200, つぼ算 ¥2,750, 試し酒 ¥3,300. The rakugo evenings three or four times a month are performed entirely in Japanese and turn on wordplay, so for a non-speaker they are a spectacle rather than a comprehensible show, but the ¥2,500 「おアトもよろしくセット」 that follows one — nibbles and two seiro — is a fine way to spend an evening. Closed Sundays, and it closes early: 14:00 for lunch, 20:15 for dinner, 19:30 on Saturdays and holidays. Shut 11–15 August, and the shop warns of irregular extra closures 「従業員の福利厚生として」, so check before making a trip. Tabelog records 予約不可 while Gnavi and the shop's LINE both take course bookings — walk in for noodles, book for a room.

enrich_note: Confirmed on the strongest evidence in this shard — a live business with its own site, a named operating company, a Mitsui Fudosan neighbourhood feature and a Shizuoka prefectural profile. The light record's name 薮伊豆総本店 and cuisine 'Soba' are both correct; only the pin was wrong, being the Nihonbashi centroid at 35.684, 139.774. The address is 〒103-0027 東京都中央区日本橋3-15-7, identical on the shop's own site, Tabelog (13006318) and Gnavi (gakp200); coordinates set to the GSI geocode of 日本橋三丁目15番7号 (35.679085, 139.775101), which sits about 12 m from Gnavi's own published WGS84 pair (35.679039, 139.775182) and agrees with Tabelog's 「日本橋駅から358m」. On dates: the house began as 伊豆本 in Kyōbashi in the Tempō era and became 薮伊豆 in 1882 on being taken under 神田やぶそば's noren, so Tabelog's オープン日 of 1882 is the Yabu-lineage date rather than the origin; it moved to Nihonbashi in the late 1990s and is on its sixth generation. The light record's gf 'ask' and vegan 'ask' are both corrected to 'no', and the gluten call is about the recipe rather than contamination: the shop states in its own words that it cuts its soba 二八, and sells a mail-order soba of 「蕎麦粉50%以上」. Currency check: the Gnavi page was last updated 17 August 2026 and lists rakugo dates through 24 October, so a published closure of 21–24 September 2026 for 設備改修 and lunch-only service on 5 September are both current, not stale. Search legs, all HTTP 200 and all read: Yahoo Japan for 「薮伊豆総本店 日本橋 そば」 and for 「薮伊豆総本店 野川 六代目 日本橋 落語」; the shop's own site (index, こだわり, お品書き, 店舗情報, 店内のご案内, お取り寄せ, 寄席); s.tabelog.com; r.gnavi.co.jp; nihonbashi-tokyo.jp; and the Shizuoka Prefecture PDF, which a server-side fetch could not parse and which was read by extracting the text locally. One caution for the merge: the representative named on the shop's mail-order page is 野川喜央 and the okami interviewed in both press pieces is 野川雅江; the sources establish that both are the family running the sixth-generation shop but do not state which of them is the sixth-generation 主人, and no reading for 喜央 is published anywhere, so the name is recorded in kanji with only the surname romanised.
